chunks: "Flying probe testing is an electrical test of a board without a custom fixture.

Instead of hundreds of probes pressed on all at once, the machine has a small number of probes, typically four to eight or more, on motorised arms that fly over the board, touch down on pads, vias or component leads, take a measurement, lift, and move to the next spot.
The program comes straight from the CAD data, so there's no tooling to build.

What it can capture is basically the structural set: shorts and opens between nets, missing or wrong components, resistor, capacitor and inductor values, diode orientation, and some limited powered checks.
You can also use it on bare boards to verify continuity against the netlist. The trade-off is speed.
Each measurement requires moving probes, so a board might take several minutes, where a bed-of-nails fixture takes seconds.
But there's no fixture cost, so for prototypes, low or medium volume, or products that change often, it wins.
It also reaches places a fixed fixture may not, because it can touch pads on both sides and tiny features.
Downsides: it can leave marks on pads, it can't test at speed, and it won't tell you whether the product functions, so I'd pair it with functional test."
